title: UConn's $32 million-plus Gampel Pavilion naming deal lands in court over a promise made in 1989
text:
Harry Gampel’s daughters say the M&T Bank deal diminishes their father’s name on the home of UConn basketball

Texas elementary school named in honor of retired custodian

Retired custodian Marilyn Hampton joins 'Fox & Friends First' to discuss her emotional reaction to having a newly constructed Texas school named in her honor. Aubrey ISD surprised Hampton by naming the Marilyn Hampton Elementary School after her to recognize her decades of dedicated service. Hampton shares how she was moved to tears by the unexpected and historic school tribute.

In 1989, Harry A. Gampel gave UConn $1 million to help build a basketball arena. The university’s president promised in writing that the building would bear Gampel’s name "in perpetuity."

Thirty-seven years later, three of Gampel’s daughters are suing over a 20-year naming deal with M&T Bank that CT Insider reported is worth $32.5 million. Margo Gampel Absher, Debra Gampel Fischman and Linda Gampel Abrahamson filed suit Nov. 11 in Hartford Superior Court against UConn’s Board of Trustees and the state of Connecticut.

An aerial view of Harry A. Gampel Pavilion, home of the UConn men's and women's basketball teams, on the University of Connecticut campus in Storrs, Conn., on Nov. 3, 2025. (Getty Images)

The sisters allege the deal violates the terms of their father’s gift by giving the bank’s name more prominence on the building. They are asking a judge to order UConn to restore prominent exterior signage bearing the full name, Harry A. Gampel Pavilion.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Richard Weinstein, the family’s attorney, told OutKick in an email that his clients "are not looking for money." He said the family wants the arena called Harry A. Gampel Pavilion at M&T Bank Center, with both names displayed in lettering of the same size. Weinstein said he presented that exact proposal to UConn but received no response.

In a statement to OutKick, UConn said it "continues to honor and revere Harry A. Gampel, his extraordinary generosity, and his legacy." The university said it plans to add backlit signs recognizing Gampel at several public entrances, new signs inside the arena and a physical tribute to Gampel and the arena’s championship history.

The university also said it communicated with representatives of Gampel family members before the announcement and has sought in-person meetings with interested family members.

"Those invitations to meet have not yet been accepted," UConn said.

Weinstein told CT Insider the family is willing to meet to negotiate equal billing, but he disputed UConn’s account of its outreach.

What UConn promised in 1989

In his Oct. 16, 1989, letter to Gampel, then-UConn President John T. Casteen III said the full name would appear on event tickets and in university publications, releases and public statements. He also described plans at the time for brass lettering above the southeast entrance and said the university would maintain signage identifying the building as Harry A. Gampel Pavilion for as long as it remained in service.

General view of the scoreboard during player introductions before the college basketball game between Maryland Terrapins and UConn Huskies on Nov. 16, 2023, at Harry A. Gampel Pavilion in Storrs, Conn. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

The arena opened in January 1990 and is the on-campus home of UConn’s men’s and women’s basketball teams. In a 2015 retrospective on the arena’s opening, UConn Athletics said the university had given Gampel "naming rights in perpetuity to the basketball arena."

It probably seemed like an easy decision at the time. Gampel’s gift was the largest private donation UConn had received. I doubt anyone in the president’s office was thinking about what a bank might pay to put its name on the same building 37 years later.

On Oct. 21, trustees voted unanimously to authorize the name "M&T Bank Center at Harry A. Gampel Pavilion" for the larger athletics complex, which houses the arena and several offices. The authorization was contingent on a signed gift agreement. M&T’s announcement said the arena would be renamed "M&T Bank Center at Gampel Pavilion." That public name omits "Harry A." from the name the trustees authorized.

Photos show the M&T Bank Center lettering above the east entrance is much larger than the Gampel Pavilion lettering below it. In a letter reported by the Hartford Courant on Nov. 7, Gampel’s daughters said they would have accepted equal billing and said UConn had not consulted them.

Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont urged the family and the trustees to resolve the dispute in remarks reported Wednesday by CT Insider.

Why $32.5 million is hard to turn down

UConn athletic director David Benedict was talking about putting a corporate name next to Gampel’s as early as July 2025. UConn Athletics said in its 2026 annual report that it committed to sharing the full $20.5 million allowed in the 2025–26 revenue-sharing year. The limit for 2026–27 has since risen to $21.58 million. At the reported price, the M&T deal averages about $1.6 million a year.

UConn guard Paige Bueckers addresses fans after her last game at Gampel Pavilion at the end of a second round game against South Dakota State in the NCAA college basketball tournament, Monday, March 24, 2025, in Storrs, Conn. (AP Photo/Jessica Hill)

I like stadium names that tell you something about the team or the city. Lambeau Field is named for a guy who helped start the Packers. Fenway Park is named for a part of Boston. Gampel Pavilion is named for a guy who helped get the place built. I’d take any of those names over whatever a sponsor is willing to put on a sign for the next 20 years.

I get why UConn took the deal. Keeping two championship-caliber rosters together in the NIL era is expensive.

But it doesn't mean I don't wish UConn had just left Gampel Pavilion alone.

Dan Zaksheske is a reporter at OutKick.
